[Retrieved 08:10 BST Thu 24 Sep — NO NEW OVERNIGHT DEVELOPMENT FOUND. This is the fullest BBC account; the new material vs yesterday's evening brief is the Badenoch and Farage reaction quotes and the deal's financial detail.]

HEADLINE: UK to review Chagos Islands deal over lack of US support, Streeting tells BBC

FACTS:
- The original agreement would see the UK cede sovereignty of the territory to Mauritius and pay an average of £101m ($136m) per year to lease back the joint UK-US military base on Diego Garcia.
- Under the 2025 deal, Britain would lease back the base for 99 years, at what the UK government said would be a net overall cost of £3.4bn. Opponents said the real cost could amount to £35bn adjusting for inflation, and risked allowing China to establish a presence on the archipelago.
- The deal, agreed under Sir Keir Starmer, was paused indefinitely in April after Trump pulled his support.
- The UK and Mauritius signed an agreement in May 2025; the final draft of the bill to hand over sovereignty had not passed Parliament.
- The "review" is not expected to constitute a formal process operating to a specific timeframe. Government sources insist Burnham's and Streeting's comments do not represent a major shift from the previous position, which was that any deal would require American support.
- Burnham had spoken to Mauritian PM Navin Ramgoolam ahead of the New York trip; an official readout said Burnham "reiterated his commitment to continue doing everything possible" along with the US to ratify the deal.
- Trump in January 2026 called the deal "an act of great stupidity" and described it as a reason "why Greenland has to be acquired"; he has previously branded it "a blight on our great ally" and "an act of total weakness".
- Britain has controlled the islands since 1814; in 1965, ahead of Mauritian independence, the Chagos Islands were made a British overseas territory and the UK paid Mauritius a £3m grant in compensation. In 1966 Britain leased Diego Garcia to the US; that arrangement expires in 2036.
- In 2019 the International Court of Justice gave an advisory opinion that Britain's separation of the Chagos Islands from Mauritius was unlawful and that the UK must end its administration as rapidly as possible. Non-binding, but endorsed by the UN General Assembly; it led to the UK opening negotiations in 2022.

QUOTE — WES STREETING, Defence Secretary (BBC Breakfast): "we have to" review the deal "because the United States doesn't support it". And: "What President Trump said yesterday wasn't new but I think it does provide absolute clarity that his position on this Chagos deal as currently drafted is not changing. So we have to do more work with our American allies, with President Trump and his administration, to get the deal to a place where he can support it."

QUOTE — WES STREETING (BBC Radio 4 Today, Wednesday): no money would be handed over to Mauritius "at this stage" while officials review the deal. He described the Diego Garcia base as "one of the most sensitive and valuable national security assets", and said work was under way to find a deal "that maybe not everyone loves, but everyone can live with".

QUOTE — ANDY BURNHAM, Prime Minister (to broadcasters): he has "inherited the situation and we need a resolution". He added: "It's critical to safeguard the future of the base, and that matters to us for security reasons, but also clearly to the United States as well. What I said in the meeting is that we will work to find that resolution between the different sides, and we'll work hard to find it."

QUOTE — DONALD TRUMP (to Burnham at UNGA): criticised the "terrible deal" and said the UK was "going to be looking" at it. Burnham replied: "Yep."

QUOTE — KEMI BADENOCH, Conservative leader (reacting to the review): called on Burnham to "just scrap this terrible deal".

QUOTE — NIGEL FARAGE, Reform UK leader: "The Chagos deal is dead. Thank God."
